paragraphs: [Shabbat 56a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.56a.13) mentions him setting two statements of Rav against one another. Hyman suggests that the Abaye reporting Rav in [Shabbat 57b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.57b.16) may be Abaye Kashisha. He recites baraitot in [Yevamot 24a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.24a.17) and [Ketubot 94a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.94a.6); in [Ketubot 96b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.96b.7) he gives Rabbi Yose’s parable beginning “What is this like?” [Sanhedrin 7a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.7a.6) preserves his saying: “A quarrel is like the planking of a bridge: once it is fixed, it stays fixed.”[^2]

notes.text: Rami is not a new speaker: the opening describes setting Rav’s statements against each other. The final proverb concerns a quarrel, not a merchant. Rashi explains the bridge-plank image as a quarrel becoming entrenched through repetition.

Shabbat 56a explicitly gives Abaye Kashisha as the sage who sets two statements of Rav against each other. At 57b the speaker transmits in Rav’s name and is called simply Abaye. Ketubot 94a mentions both Abaye and Abaye Kashisha. Heilprin lists the named Kashisha passages. See [Heilprin’s corresponding entry](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=136&lang=en).
